parts.label: (a)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what must happen for a force to do work - does the object just feel a force, or must it also move in a particular direction relative to that force?
parts.proper_answer: Work done is the product of the force and the displacement in the direction of the force, $W = Fd\cos\theta$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Work Really Means**
Think of pushing a box along the floor. You feel you have done work only if the box actually moves. If you push hard on a wall that does not move, no work is done. So work links force and motion together.

Step 2: **The Precise Definition**
Work is done when a force causes displacement. Only the component of displacement along the line of the force counts. In symbols: $$W = F \times d \text{ in direction of } F$$ If the force is at an angle $\theta$ to motion, use $W = Fd\cos\theta$. Its unit is the joule $\text{J}$.

(b)(i)
parts.part_stem: For the carriage moving from X to Y

markscheme_points.text: using a micrometer / digital calipers; several measurements in different places

hints: Hint 1: Focus on the starting and finishing motion - you know mass and two different speeds, so what expression gives the stored motion energy at X and at Y separately?
Hint 2: Work out the two $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ values and subtract final from initial, keeping enough figures to show the result rounds to $9.9 \times 10^4\text{ J}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find Energy At Each Point**
You have the same mass $m = 580\text{ kg}$ but different speeds. Kinetic energy is $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$. So calculate it twice, once with $v_X = 22\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and once with $v_Y = 12\text{ m s}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Take The Decrease**
$$E_{kX} = \frac{1}{2} \times 580 \times 22^2 = 140360\text{ J}$$ $$E_{kY} = \frac{1}{2} \times 580 \times 12^2 = 41760\text{ J}$$ Decrease = initial - final: $$\Delta E_k = 140360 - 41760 = 98600\text{ J} \approx 9.9 \times 10^4\text{ J}$$ This confirms the given value.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Show that the length of the track from X to Y is $20\text{ m}$.
hints: Hint 1: Look at the right angle in Fig. 2.1 - what fraction of a full circle is the arc XY with radius $13\text{ m}$?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recognise A Quarter Circle**
The two $13\text{ m}$ lines are perpendicular, so XY subtends $90^{\circ}$ at the centre. That is one quarter of a full circle.

Step 2: **Quarter Circumference**
Full circumference $= 2\pi r$. So: $$L = \frac{1}{4} \times 2\pi r = \frac{\pi r}{2} = \frac{\pi \times 13}{2} \approx 20.4\text{ m} \approx 20\text{ m}$$

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Use your answers in (b)(i) and (b)(ii) to calculate the average resistive force acting on the carriage as it moves from X to Y.
hints: Hint 1: Compare your two energy numbers - the kinetic energy lost is bigger than the gravitational energy gained, so where must the missing energy have gone?
Hint 2: That missing energy equals work done against resistance, $F \times d$, where $d$ is the $20\text{ m}$ track length - how can you rearrange to find $F$?
parts.proper_answer: Work against resistance $= 9.9 \times 10^4 - 7.4 \times 10^4 = 2.5 \times 10^4\text{ J}$. $F = W/d = 2.5 \times 10^4 / 20.4 \approx 1.2\text{-}1.3 \times 10^3\text{ N}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Do An Energy Balance**
With no friction all lost kinetic energy would become potential energy. Here some is lost heating the track and air. So: $$\text{loss in } E_k = \text{gain in } E_p + \text{work against resistance}$$

Step 2: **Find Average Resistive Force**
Work against resistance: $$W_R = 9.9 \times 10^4 - 7.4 \times 10^4 \approx 2.5 \times 10^4\text{ J}$$ This work equals $F_{avg} \times d$ with $d \approx 20.4\text{ m}$: $$F_{avg} = \frac{W_R}{d} = \frac{2.5 \times 10^4}{20.4} \approx 1.2 \times 10^3\text{ N}$$ Using $d = 20\text{ m}$ gives about $1300\text{ N}$. The force opposes motion along the track.

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.text: Describe the change in the direction of the linear momentum of the carriage as it moves from X to Y.

markscheme_points.text: from horizontal / right to vertical / up

hints: Hint 1: Momentum points the same way as velocity - compare the arrow at X with the stated motion at Y in the text.
parts.proper_answer: Direction changes from horizontal (to the right) at X to vertical (upwards) at Y, through $90^{\circ}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Momentum Follows Velocity**
Momentum $p = mv$ is a vector in the same direction as velocity. At X the carriage moves horizontally to the right, so $p$ is to the right.

Step 2: **Turn Through 90 Degrees**
At Y the carriage moves vertically upwards. So the direction of momentum has rotated from horizontal to vertical, a $90^{\circ}$ change.

parts.label: (b)(v)
parts.text: Determine the magnitude of the change in linear momentum when the carriage moves from X to Y.
hints: Hint 1: Start by finding the size of the momentum vector at X and at Y separately using $p = mv$ - what are the two magnitudes and their directions?
Hint 2: Since change is final minus initial and the two vectors are at right angles, sketch them tail to tail and think what geometric rule gives the length of the difference vector.
Hint 3: Combine the two perpendicular momenta with Pythagoras, $\Delta p = \sqrt{p_X^2 + p_Y^2}$, and evaluate to about $10^4\text{ N s}$.
parts.proper_answer: $p_X = 580 \times 22 = 12760\text{ N s}$, $p_Y = 580 \times 12 = 6960\text{ N s}$. $\Delta p = \sqrt{p_X^2 + p_Y^2} \approx 1.5 \times 10^4\text{ N s}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Calculate The Two Momenta**
Momentum magnitude is $p = mv$. $$p_X = 580 \times 22 = 12760\text{ N s horizontal}$$ $$p_Y = 580 \times 12 = 6960\text{ N s vertical}$$ A common mistake is to just subtract the numbers. You cannot, because they are in different directions.

Step 2: **Vector Change**
Change $= \vec{p}_Y - \vec{p}_X$. Because the vectors are perpendicular, the magnitude of the difference is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle: $$|\Delta \vec{p}| = \sqrt{p_X^2 + p_Y^2}$$

Step 3: **Evaluate**
$$|\Delta p| = \sqrt{12760^2 + 6960^2} = \sqrt{1.63 \times 10^8 + 4.84 \times 10^7} \approx 1.45 \times 10^4\text{ N s} \approx 1.5 \times 10^4\text{ N s}$$ Direction is diagonally between the negative horizontal and positive vertical, but only magnitude is asked for.

hints: Hint 1: The carriage climbs from X up to Y - look at Fig. 2.1 to spot the vertical height risen, not the distance along the curved track.

walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot The Height Gain**
From Fig. 2.1 the centre of the circle is $13\text{ m}$ above X and $13\text{ m}$ to the left of Y. So Y is $h = 13\text{ m}$ vertically above X. The curved distance does not matter for gravitational potential.

Step 2: **Apply mgh**
Gravitational potential gain is: $$\Delta E_p = mgh$$ $$\Delta E_p = 580 \times 9.81 \times 13 = 73967\text{ J} \approx 7.4 \times 10^4\text{ J}$$
